subtype: Approach: hiding worry and carrying it alone [Pitfall]
passage:
"Tarun, your Maths test. Amma found it in your bag. Thirty-one?"
"It's fine, Akka. One bad test."
"You got eighty-five last term. And you're awake at two every night. I can see the light under your door."
"Just studying."
"You're not studying. You're staring at the ceiling." Gopika sat on his bed. "Is this about Appa's shop?"
Tarun said nothing for a long moment. "I heard them talking about the rent. I didn't want to add to it."
"So you've been carrying it alone for a month?"
"They've got enough to worry about. They don't need to worry about me too."
"Tarun, they are worrying about you. They think you've stopped caring about school. They have no idea why."
He looked down at the test paper. "I thought keeping quiet was helping."

qa.q: What did Tarun score on the Maths test?
qa.a: Thirty-one.

qa.q: What has Tarun been feeling for the past month?
qa.a: He has been anxious and weighed down, lying awake at night and carrying the worry about the shop's rent alone.

qa.q: What could Tarun do now instead of keeping quiet?
qa.a: Tell Amma and Appa what he overheard and how it has affected him, so they can reassure him and explain what is really happening.

qa.q: How do Amma and Appa see Tarun's falling marks?
qa.a: They think he has stopped caring about school, with no idea he has been silently worrying about the family's money.

grounding: A dialogue shows a teen hiding worry about money at home while stress builds and marks fall, and his parents misreading it.

subtype: Approach: hiding worry and carrying it alone [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Leela, and for most of Class 10 I pretended everything was normal. After Papa's contract ended, I heard Mummy crying on the phone to Nani about the school fees. I decided the best thing I could do was not be a problem. So I smiled at dinner, said school was "good", and didn't mention that I'd stopped sleeping properly. I did homework at midnight because I couldn't focus in the evenings. My Science marks dropped from the eighties to the fifties. When Samir, my bench partner, asked if I was okay, I snapped at him. My parents thought I'd just got lazy, and there were arguments about my marks, which made it worse. Nobody could help with a worry nobody knew about. I was protecting them from something they were already carrying.

qa.q: How far did Leela's Science marks drop?
qa.a: From the eighties to the fifties.

qa.q: Why did Leela snap at Samir?
qa.a: Leela was anxious and exhausted from holding the worry in, so Samir's question hit a sore spot.

qa.q: What would have helped Leela carry the worry better?
qa.a: Telling Mummy and Papa what was overheard and how it felt, so they could reassure Leela and share the load.

qa.q: How did Leela's parents see the falling marks?
qa.a: They thought Leela had become lazy, which led to arguments, because they didn't know about the hidden worry.

grounding: A teen recalls hiding worry about family money, stress building and marks falling while parents could not help.

subtype: Approach: exploring scholarships and school support [Action]
passage: Harish kanna, you think asking for help is shameful? Let your Lakshmi Paati tell you something. When I was fifteen, my father's mill closed, and I thought I'd have to leave school. I cried for two days. Then I went to my class teacher, Miss Rosamma, after the bell and asked straight out: is there any help for girls whose families can't pay? She told me about the fee concession and a state scholarship, and that the forms were due in three weeks. My father and I spent two evenings at the taluk office getting the income certificate. I copied my mark sheets out neatly by hand. We handed it all in five days early. I got both. That is how your Paati finished school, kanna. The help existed. I only had to ask for it.

subtype: Approach: exploring scholarships and school support [Action]

Papa's work has been less since the summer." Pallavi Ma'am read the notice, then wrote out a checklist: mark sheet, income certificate, ID proof, bank details. "The fee concession forms are in the office too. Take both." That evening Trisha and her mother emptied the steel trunk of files onto the floor and found everything but the certificate. Her mother phoned Papa, who told them which folder. On Thursday afternoon, a day early, Trisha handed in both forms, every line of the checklist ticked.

subtype: Approach: comparing free resources for study [Thinking]
passage: Harsha, you're upset you can't join that coaching centre? Listen to your Ramesh Mama. I sat on the steps of the temple tank one evening and listed everything I could get free. The school library, open till five. Our Physics teacher, who stayed back for doubts on Wednesdays. My neighbour's son, a year senior, who still had his notes. The government's free lessons on television in the evening. And three friends who also weren't going to coaching. Then I asked myself which ones matched how I learn. Library and doubts for Physics. The senior's notes for Chemistry. A study group for Maths, because I learn by arguing. The television lessons I dropped. I passed with a first class.

subtype: Approach: demanding things regardless of family condition [Pitfall]

Madhav bhai,
You asked if I got the new running shoes, the ones the whole team has. Short answer: no. Long answer: I've been a bit of an idiot. Papa's hours were cut in June. I knew that. But every evening for two weeks I kept bringing up the shoes: everyone has them, I'll look like a loser at the district meet, you don't care. Last Friday it turned into a shouting match, and I saw Mummy go into the kitchen and not come out for a long time. Papa said sorry to me, as if it was his fault. That felt worse than not having the shoes. I keep thinking, I'm always the one saying things should be fair, and I wasn't being fair at all. My old ones still run. I'm going to tell them that tonight.
Deepak

I gave some of it to Amma for vegetables and kept some in a tin marked "exam fees". When the board registration came, the tin covered it. I was so proud. subtype: Approach: budget planning with parents [Action]
passage: In Pranav's village the harvest money came twice a year, and this year the rains had been poor. For weeks his parents had talked in low voices after dinner. One night Bapu surprised him: "Pranav, bring your notebook. You're good with numbers." They sat on the charpai with a lantern. Bapu said what came in each month from the dairy. Aai listed what had to go out: the electricity, the tractor loan instalment, school fees, cattle feed. Pranav wrote it in two columns. What was left was small, but it was there on the page. Then they planned the rest together: no new clothes till Diwali, and Mohit's cycle repair first, because he rode it to school. Pranav noticed his chest felt lighter. The number was small, but it was known. Mohit, listening from his mat, asked if his cycle was really first.

subtype: Approach: budget planning with parents [Action]

Her mother listed rent, electricity, the bus passes, the phone. Rosa did the subtraction. What was left looked small. Then they planned the rest: groceries first, a little for Rosa's school trip in spring, nothing for takeaway pizza. "Can we keep this on the fridge?" Rosa asked. Her father looked surprised, then nodded. For the first time in weeks, she slept straight through the night.

A few days later the schedule changed: only Dolma and one other child, only at weekends. Her father went to the school office to ask about the fee concession, and her mother told mine, "Her studies come first. We'll manage the rest another way." I can't say how Dilnaz felt. But the light in her room went off by ten after that.

qa.a: It suggests she was exhausted and overstretched, with tutoring eating into her sleep.

qa.a: The narrator noticed the lighter schedule and the light going off by ten, while not knowing how Dilnaz felt inside.

subtype: Approach: reframing shame into resourcefulness [Revision]
passage: Hrithik, you've been hiding that you can't go on the trip? Sit. Your Francis Uncle has a story. In Class 11, after my father's shop shut, I was so ashamed. I wore my shoes till the soles flapped and told everyone I liked them broken in. I skipped every outing with some excuse. My football coach, Mr D'Costa, noticed. One evening he asked why I'd stopped coming to team dinners. I told him, eyes on the ground. He said, "Francis, you know how to make one pair of shoes last three years, and cook for your brothers on almost nothing. That's a skill. Most grown men can't do it." I had never thought of it like that. The next week I told my best friend, Joe, the truth. He just said, "Okay. Then we'll eat at my place."

qa.a: Joe was calm and kind, simply offering to eat at his place, showing the truth didn't change the friendship.

subtype: Approach: reframing shame into resourcefulness [Revision]

subtype: Approach: working backward from the date [Thinking]

subtype: Approach: working backward from the date [Thinking]

Olga, who had been planning to "sort it as we go", watched the column fill. "So if we miss the hall date, everything else shifts." "Exactly. The date doesn't move. We do." subtype: Approach: budget and resource planning [Action]
